Design premise
A film environment that invites visitors with different visual abilities to encounter cinema through the whole body.

What does it mean to experience a film when vision is no longer its primary medium?

SYNAETHESIA is a speculative cinema in Detroit designed with visually impaired audiences in mind. Rather than treating film as an exclusively visual medium, the project explores how tactile surfaces, changes in temperature, scent, acoustic atmosphere, and movement through space can become parallel ways of interpreting a cinematic narrative.

The architecture is conceived as a sequence of sensory encounters. Visitors move from transitional spaces into the screening room, library, garden, and workshop—each offering a different relationship between body, environment, and moving image.

Spatial transitions become as important as the film itself: an atmosphere might be felt as warmth or coolness, a memory might be evoked through fragrance, and orientation might come from textures and carefully arranged circulation.

01 / EXPERIMENTS IN PERCEPTION

Seeing through other senses

Three image sequences explore how familiar scenes change when reduced, blurred, and translated into heightened fields of color and contrast.

These experiments begin with ordinary images: a garden path, a crowded street, and an interior corridor. As definition is removed, patterns of luminance and chromatic intensity become newly prominent. The resulting visual language provides an opening for the design inquiry, rather than pretending to represent any single person’s vision.

“A film can be more than something we watch. It can be something we physically inhabit.”
02 / DESIGN STRATEGIES

Constructing a sensory landscape

Environmental strategies connect access, microclimate, shaded movement, and planting with a cinema that is experienced across multiple senses.

01 / TouchTactile surfaces and transitions offer cues to movement, encounter, and orientation.
02 / TemperatureWarmth, cooling, sunlight, and microclimate extend the atmosphere of cinema into the building.
03 / ScentPlanting and indoor gardens suggest how memory and narrative might emerge through smell.
03 / ARCHITECTURAL DOCUMENTS

A cinema organized by experience

Plans and sections show the building’s sequence from public arrival to immersive screening and enclosed sensory spaces.

The ground floor creates a sequence of public thresholds and accessible circulation, while spaces below accommodate the main screening environment alongside workshops and a film library. The circular cinema anchors the project; adjoining rooms and the garden expand the cinematic experience beyond the screen.

04 / ATMOSPHERIC STUDIES

The body as an audience

The final four visualizations trace the visitor experience from the theater into a series of sensory and social spaces.

In the screening room, a tall cylindrical surface places moving images at the center of an immersive space. The design imagines an audience gathered not around a conventional front-facing screen, but around shared sensations that can be interpreted in different ways.

Between the screening environments, circulation is also an active design element. Continuous lighting along edges, changes in material character, and tactile surfaces help establish an atmosphere that is legible through more than sight alone.

SYNAETHESIA approaches accessibility as a generative design question. Its goal is not simply to accommodate visual impairment after the fact, but to ask what cinema—and its architecture—might become when people with different sensory experiences are considered from the beginning.
